quote: Every Utopia ever constructed—in philosophy, fiction, or religion—has been, to one degree or another, a place where you wouldn’t actually want to live.
content: "To one degree or another" makes the claim unfalsifiable, since any imagined place with any flaw qualifies. Taken at face value, it is false. Iain M. Banks's Culture novels depict a post-scarcity civilization that Banks said he would like to live in, and many readers say the same. The heavens of the major religions are places their believers do want to go. The Orwell essay cited is about socialists' difficulty depicting happiness, not a survey of utopias. A claim about "every Utopia ever constructed" requires at least a look at the ones built to be livable.

quote: George Orwell said much the same thing in “Why Socialists Don’t Believe In Fun,”
content: The essay appeared in Tribune in December 1943 under the pseudonym "John Freeman," titled "Can Socialists Be Happy?"; "Why Socialists Don't Believe in Fun" is a later title. More importantly, Orwell doesn't conclude that utopia is impossible. He concludes that "the real objective of Socialism is not happiness," which he treats as a by-product, but human brotherhood. That is a claim about what the goal should be, and the essay doesn't engage it.

quote: Is there a single story on the list that isn’t tragic?
content: The author chose the list, and comedy is simply absent from it: Aristophanes, Shakespeare's comedies, Austen, Wodehouse. Research on why people choose sad stories doesn't support "happiness can't shout loud enough." Audiences who seek out tragic films say they do so for meaning, insight and connection, not for the pain itself (Oliver & Raney 2011). People seek entertainment that is meaningful, not just pleasurable, which fits the essay's eventual thesis better than the story about pain's intensity it tells here.

quote: The experimental rule is that losing a desideratum—$50, a coffee mug, whatever— hurts between 2 and 2.5 times as much as the equivalent gain.
content: The average figure has survived; its generality hasn't. A meta-analysis of 607 estimates finds a mean loss-aversion coefficient of about 1.96 (Brown et al. 2024), close to the essay's number. But individual estimates depend heavily on the range of gains and losses the experimenter offers, and can be made to disappear or reverse (Walasek & Stewart 2015). The coffee-mug endowment effect disappears when procedures control for subjects' misunderstandings (Plott & Zeiler 2005). And the explanation just before the number ("If losses weren't more aversive than gains, we'd go broke") is an untested evolutionary story.

quote: I expect that it takes a highly talented and experienced sexual artist working for hours to produce a good feeling as intense as the pain of one strong kick in the testicles
content: The claimed asymmetry is plausible and has some support, though the essay's evidence is an anecdote about a euphemism. Neuroscience finds that the brain's "liking" hotspots are small and fragile compared with the systems for pain and aversion (Berridge & Kringelbach 2015). The "bad is stronger than good" review gathered many areas of life in which negative events outweigh positive ones (Baumeister et al. 2001). That review predates the replication crisis and mixes very different kinds of study, so it is suggestive rather than decisive. On this point the essay is closer to right than wrong.

quote: There are people today who “suffer” from congenital analgesia—a total absence of pain. I never heard that insufficient pleasure becomes intolerable to them.
content: The case is stronger now than when this was written. Jo Cameron, identified in 2019, carries a small deletion in the FAAH-OUT pseudogene. She feels little pain, has low anxiety and an unusually positive mood, and shows no apparent intolerance of ordinary pleasures (Habib et al. 2019). She is a real human instance of the reconfiguration Pearce proposed. The more common congenital insensitivity to pain has costs the essay understates. Mutations that disable the sodium channel Nav1.7 abolish smell as well as pain (Weiss et al. 2011), and people who have them suffer frequent, often serious, unnoticed injuries. Deleting pain is possible; deleting it without collateral losses is an unsolved engineering problem.

quote: No child sexual abuse that turns out more abusers.
content: The "cycle of abuse" is weaker than this phrase implies. Most sexually abused children never become sexual offenders. In a prospective study of court-substantiated cases, the raised risk of later arrest for sex crimes was not specific to childhood sexual abuse; physically abused and neglected children showed comparable increases (Widom & Massey 2015). The harm the essay wants to eliminate is real. The causal chain it names is weaker than it implies.
